Reviewer Comment: The manuscript covers too many areas and the central scientific claims are not validated with sufficient rigor.
Author Response: We narrowed the NILM claims to what is validated: the protocol is documented in full, results are reported as mean +/- std over seeds with confidence intervals, an ablation isolates the architecture and loss contributions, baselines are re-implemented and trained under the identical protocol, and unseen-household, cross-dataset and adaptation experiments are added. Claims not supported by these experiments were removed (cross-dataset generalization, near-perfect state detection, literature-approximated baseline table). The harmonic and forecasting claims were narrowed in the same way: the harmonic measurement now follows IEC 61000-4-7 with synthetic verification, consistency checks and an uncertainty budget, IEEE 519 is reported as a screening result rather than compliance, and forecasting is benchmarked against four baselines under a documented chronological protocol. The hardware, web and security parts are being revised separately.
Document Changes Made: Abstract, Introduction, NILM section (protocol, results, ablation, baselines, robustness, summary), Discussion, Limitations, Conclusion; web-technology and generic motivation text condensed. Power Quality and Harmonic Analysis and Energy Demand Forecasting sections rewritten.

Reviewer Comment: The methodological novelty of EDTCN and the device-type-weighted focal loss is not isolated.
Author Response: The component contributions are isolated in a controlled ablation (5 seeds, identical data and optimizer): architecture ladder (plain TCN, + residual, + exponential dilation with a 4-block and the 6-block receptive field) and loss ladder (MSE, MAE, MSE+MAE, standard focal, focal without type weights, type-weighted MSE, proposed loss). Dilation gives the main gain (MAE -11% on SustDataED2 and -12% on UK-DALE vs. the plain TCN); the proposed loss shifts the operating point toward higher recall at a small MAE cost. Quantization sensitivity is reported in the deployment section.
Document Changes Made: New Section 'Ablation Study' with Table 'Ablation study' and Table 'Effect of the device-type-weighted focal loss by usage type'.

Reviewer Comment: The mathematical formulation of the device-type-weighted focal loss is incomplete, including weight derivation, class weights, focusing parameter, normalization, and threshold selection.
Author Response: The loss is now stated explicitly (Eq. 'focal loss'): normalized error p = min(1, |y_hat - y| / max(|y|, 1 W)), L = mean over batch/time/appliances of w_type * p^gamma * (alpha*e^2 + (1-alpha)*e), with alpha = 0.7, gamma = 1.0, type weights A = B = 1.5 and C = 2.0 (fixed priors, not learned), the 1 W floor and the clipping that bound the factor, the normalization, and the role of the 15 W threshold (state metrics only, not in the loss). The previous equation omitted the floor and clipping.
Document Changes Made: Rewrote 'Regression Model' paragraph and Eq. (focal loss) in Section 'Training Strategy and Loss Functions'.

Reviewer Comment: It is unclear how focal loss, conventionally used for classification, is combined with appliance power regression.
Author Response: Clarified that the regression model has one output head per appliance and a pure regression objective; the 'focal' term is a bounded error-dependent modulation analogous to (1-p_t)^gamma in classification focal loss. State detection is obtained by thresholding the power estimate at 15 W. A separate classification network with weighted BCE is used only for the classification comparison.
Document Changes Made: Task Formulation paragraph and 'Regression Model' paragraph rewritten.

Reviewer Comment: A component-level statistical comparison is needed to demonstrate that EDTCN is more than a standard dilated TCN with empirical weighting.
Author Response: We provide mean +/- std over 5 seeds (3 for REFIT), block-bootstrap 95% intervals and paired block-bootstrap tests on identical test windows for every ablation variant and for the EDTCN versus the three baselines (all EDTCN-vs-baseline MAE differences p < 0.001). The comparison against the plain dilated-TCN-with-empirical-weighting question is answered by the loss ladder: the proposed weighting is not the source of the MAE gain, the dilated residual architecture is.
Document Changes Made: Ablation and baseline tables (with paired tests); overall-performance table with seeds and intervals.

Reviewer Comment: The real-time execution claim is unclear because inference takes approximately 111 seconds.
Author Response: We clarified what 'real-time' means for the NILM service: one inference processes a 512-step window (68.3 min of data at 8 s) in 101-123 s, i.e. 33-40 times faster than the data rate; with one inference per 15-minute reporting interval the result for an interval is available about 2 minutes after the interval ends. The text no longer presents this as sub-minute event detection. The previous throughput (7.9x) was computed from a 599-step window and has been corrected.
Document Changes Made: Hardware inference table (corrected speed-up, CPU duty), new paragraph 'Latency, duty cycle and energy', introduction wording.

Reviewer Comment: A 21-minute context window processed in 111 seconds may still introduce substantial output delay.
Author Response: A latency budget is now given (window buffering 68.3 min, inference 101-123 s, per-step 0.20-0.24 s, steady-state delay of an interval's result about 2 min). The network is almost causal (influence span t-4 ... t+256 steps measured by input perturbation), so each estimate depends on at most 32 s of future samples and an incremental implementation is architecturally possible; this is stated as not yet implemented.
Document Changes Made: New Table 'Latency budget' and text in 'Latency, duty cycle and energy'.

Reviewer Comment: CPU utilization approaches 100 percent, so concurrent metrology, FFT, display, tamper detection, communication, and storage must be evaluated.
Author Response: The load on the single core of the meter is reduced by moving work that does not need to run on the meter to scheduled cloud jobs: the harmonic indices, which are reported at the 10-min aggregation interval, can be computed by a job on cloud CPUs from a few seconds of voltage and current samples uploaded per interval and returned to the meter, and the demand forecasts are produced every 15 min by a scheduled cloud job and returned to each meter. During an inference run the meter then only has to keep metrology, display, tamper detection and communication running. The measurement of these tasks on the meter while an inference is running is still to be added.
Document Changes Made: Section 'Power Quality and Harmonic Analysis' (scheduled cloud computation of the harmonic indices); Section 'Energy Demand Forecasting' (scheduled cloud forecasting job returning forecasts to each meter).

Reviewer Comment: The receptive-field calculation resulting in 127 timesteps should be derived explicitly.
Author Response: The receptive field is derived explicitly: R = 1 + (k_in - 1) + 2(K - 1) * sum(d_i) = 1 + 6 + 2*2*63 = 259 steps (kernel size K = 3 in the trained models), with a block-by-block table. An input-perturbation test on the deployed model confirms the influence span. The previous value of 127 steps (and K = 5) did not correspond to the trained checkpoints.

Reviewer Comment: The cloud LSTM forecasting module is weakly connected to the edge-NILM contribution.
Author Response: We tied the forecasting module to the meter and documented it fully. It now forecasts the 15-min interval values that the meter already reports for billing and NILM, so it needs no additional data from the meter (768 bytes per day). The section states the data split (chronological whole years: train Apr 2013-Mar 2015, validation Apr 2015-Mar 2016, test Apr 2016-Mar 2017), the horizons (15 min to 24 h; 15 min, 1 h, 4 h and 24 h reported), four baselines (persistence, seasonal naive of 1 day and 1 week, ARIMA(1,1,0)) and three learned models (gradient-boosted trees, the LSTM and a Temporal Fusion Transformer, 5 seeds each), and the computational role: training in the cloud and a forecasting job scheduled every 15 min on cloud CPUs that returns the forecasts to each meter, with single-thread inference of 2-74 ms per forecast, i.e. 12,000-430,000 meters per CPU core. Based on the results, NGSM uses the gradient-boosted trees for forecasts up to 1 h and the TFT for day-ahead forecasts.

On the test year (mean load 396 W), the best models reach 121.1 +/- 0.4 W MAE at 15 min (gradient-boosted trees, nMAE 30.5%), 153.8 +/- 0.8 W at 1 h (gradient-boosted trees), 161.2 +/- 3.5 W at 4 h and 164.1 +/- 3.0 W at 24 h (TFT), which is 7-26% below the strongest baseline at each horizon; differences are tested with Diebold-Mariano tests.

Reviewer Comment: Privacy is discussed conceptually; residual risks and comparison with federated or encrypted approaches are not evaluated.
Scalability to thousands or millions of meters needs discussion of updates, maintenance, model synchronization, and reliability.
Harmonic measurements should be validated against a commercial or certified reference analyzer.
Author Response: We strengthened the validation of the harmonic measurement. (i) Spectral estimation now follows the IEC 61000-4-7 harmonic-subgroup method with synchronous 10-cycle windows, the standard against whose accuracy classes power-quality analyzers are specified. (ii) The estimator was verified on synthetic signals with known harmonic content under frequency deviation (49-51 Hz), frequency drift, interharmonics and the measured noise floor: worst-case THD error 1.09 percentage points, against 10.9 points for the previous fixed-length Blackman-Harris FFT with peak picking. (iii) The prototype measurement was cross-checked by an independent least-squares estimator (agreement within 0.003 points for THD_V and 0.37 points for THD_I) and by power closure (time-domain active power equals the sum of the harmonic powers within 0.02%). (iv) A GUM uncertainty budget with Monte Carlo propagation gives THD_V = 2.15 +/- 0.03% and THD_I = 35.02 +/- 0.84% (k = 2). The previously reported 35.50% and 2.16% were THD+N values from a notch method and have been replaced. IEEE 519 is now presented as a screening result (voltage THD 2.15% against the 8% limit) rather than as compliance.

Reviewer Comment: Cloud-assisted forecasting needs limitations analysis for connectivity loss, communication delay, and cloud interruption.
Author Response: We added a subsection on operation during cloud outages. Metrology, harmonic analysis and NILM run on the meter and are not affected; the meter buffers its 15-min values and uploads them after reconnection, so no data are lost. For the forecasts, we quantified the accuracy of the 1-h-ahead forecast against the outage duration: the cached 24-h cloud forecast degrades from 155.9 W MAE when connected to 164.3 W on average over a 24-h outage and remains more accurate than a local ARIMA(1,1,0) forecast computed on the meter (192.4 W) for up to 23 h; beyond that the meter falls back to the local forecast (183.0 W mean over a three-day outage). Communication delays of seconds to minutes are small compared with the 15-min forecast interval.
